name: Fracturework — Shelf Broken-Chrome Art Movement
description: Fracturework artists salvage damaged, discarded, and non-functional cyberware and augmentation hardware from Shelf scrap markets and illegal strip operations, assembling them into large-scale public installations that comment on the violence of aug culture's discard economy — the chrome that gets left behind when someone can't afford maintenance, or gets stripped from the dead. The movement's aesthetic is deliberately ugly by chrome-pride standards: rust, exposed wiring, cracked optical lenses arranged into faces, skeletal wall-reliefs made from prosthetic limbs. Their most famous piece, the Thousand-Arm Wall on the south face of the Caldwell Overpass, Tier 1, is forty meters of fused prosthetic limbs that has survived three corporate removal attempts. Members are identified by a small patch of deliberately unpolished chrome worn somewhere visible.
cultural_impact: Fracturework has made the material reality of aug disposal visible in a way that corporate media consistently suppresses, and their installations have become pilgrimage sites for both Shelf residents and curious Tier 3 visitors who document and spread images through uncensored Underworld channels. The movement has created a secondary market for scrap chrome that has complicated corporate recycling contracts.
locations: Thousand-Arm Wall, Caldwell Overpass south face, Tier 1
The Stripped, a collective workshop in a gutted transit depot, Tier 1
Scrap Mile, informal scavenging corridor along Shelf industrial edge
story_hooks: The Thousand-Arm Wall has been tagged for demolition by a corponation claiming the overpass structure is unsafe — Fracturework suspects the real reason is that a piece of chrome embedded in the wall contains a still-active memory core from a corporate executive's illegally discarded augmentation.

A Tier 4 art collector has begun purchasing Fracturework pieces through intermediaries and displaying them in private — the movement is divided between those who see this as validation and those who see it as the ultimate co-optation of their anti-corporate message.

Someone is planting Fracturework-style installations in Tier 3 and 4 neighborhoods containing hidden surveillance devices, and the real Fracturework collective is being blamed for corporate espionage they didn't commit.
